stories.summary: Ajay explains the old Indian 'national' firm through the East India Company. Clive did his own thing because no email could reach him, and Indian branch managers until the 1980s were the same: regional satraps who had to be empowered because they couldn't check back with HQ. Once computers and telecom arrived, Robert Clive was under daily surveillance from HQ.
stories.insight: How far authority can be centralised depends on the communication technology of the day. Without connectivity, decentralisation is forced on a firm, along with discretion, sloppy process and petty corruption. With connectivity, central control becomes possible.
stories.quote: I always like to remind everybody that Robert Clive did his own thing because there was no email.

stories.topic: Pleading With Indian Airlines Staff and the Demigod Branch Manager
stories.summary: Ajay's defining image of the old era is a customer earnestly arguing with an Indian Airlines frontline employee. It made sense, because those employees really did have discretion. In banks, the teller had little power, but the branch manager was 'like a demigod' who made genuinely important decisions, so it was worth arguing with him.
stories.insight: Whom you bother persuading shows you where power sits inside an organisation. In the old Indian firm it sat at the local front line, which allowed sensible local adaptation and also local bias and corruption.
stories.quote: Actually, the frontline employees of Indian Airlines had a lot of discretion. They could do many things. They were seriously powerful people.

stories.topic: The Customer Yelling at Amazon Customer Care
stories.summary: While working at a Starbucks, Amit overheard a woman at the next table lose her temper with Amazon customer care and declare she would never buy from the company again. He thought it was pointless, since the agent was following a script and couldn't help her. Ajay's story then gave him the explanation: the habit dates from an era when frontline staff could actually change outcomes.
stories.insight: Habits formed under one organisational design outlive it. Customers still try to argue with frontline staff who no longer have any discretion.
stories.quote: But this kind of explains why that habit would have been there.

stories.topic: Maggi and Kit Kat Taste Different in Every Country
stories.summary: Ajay noticed that Maggi noodles taste different in Indonesia, India and the UK. Nestle runs focus groups and R&D to tune the flavour for each country, such as Thailand versus Indonesia versus India. Kit Kat varies the same way. Kit Kat fans revere the British original. Americans are stuck with a sugar-loaded version pushed by Hershey's. Japanese Kit Kats are legendary, and travellers carry bagfuls home.
stories.insight: Global firms already treat each country as its own product market. Ajay asks why Indian firms then sell one Maggi, or run one home-loan algorithm, across a country as diverse as India.
stories.quote: The original British Kit Kat is perfect. Kit Kats in Japan are magical. Kit Kat in America are horrible.

stories.summary: When CMIE's algorithm divided India into homogeneous regions, Kerala came out as three: North, Central and South. Ajay discussed this with many people who know Kerala, and they agreed. The three parts really do differ in important ways, and three is the right level of detail, not ten.
stories.insight: Even a small, seemingly uniform state contains several distinct markets. The useful level of detail is a judgement call: fine enough to show real differences, coarse enough to stay usable.
stories.quote: There's North Kerala, there's central Kerala, and there's South Kerala.

stories.topic: 5x Income, 18x Phones: Homework for the Kelkar–Shah Book
stories.summary: For the decentralisation chapter of In Service of the Republic, Ajay compared CMIE's 100 homogeneous regions. The richest region is about 5.3 times richer than the poorest. The number that stayed with him was the share of women who own a mobile phone, which captures household prosperity, social progressiveness and willingness to give a teenage girl a phone. That share is about 18 times higher in the top regions than in the bottom ones.
stories.insight: A single well-chosen indicator can reveal how far apart India's regions are socially, which an all-India average hides completely.
stories.quote: And it turns out that the highest values in India are like 18 times higher than the lowest values

stories.topic: Bank of America's Tiny India in 1991
stories.summary: In 1991 Bank of America took more interest in India than it does today. Even so, its entire Indian operation was about the size of its business in some small US state, because India was too poor to support much.
stories.insight: Tailoring a product or process to a region has fixed costs, and a small market can't pay them. As Indian markets for loans, noodles and chocolate grow, the case for regional customisation gets stronger.
stories.quote: But the entire aggregate Indian operations were like some tiny small state of the United States because India was so poor that whatever you could do in India was more limited.

stories.topic: South Indian Firms Cursing the North
stories.summary: Ajay knows firms that are comfortable operating in South India and dismiss North India as a wasteland they can't and won't operate in. His answer is to hire people who understand the North and work out how to compete there. The upside is real, even if the tidy, calm southern playbook won't work.
stories.insight: When a firm calls a market 'too difficult', it is often describing the limits of its own understanding. Those gaps are where other firms find room.
stories.quote: And they will mutter strange curses and say North India is some wasteland and I don't know how to operate there and I won't operate there.

stories.topic: Credit Scores From Caps Lock and Battery Levels
stories.summary: Amit recalls his episode with Rahul Matthan and Matthan's book. Lenders are using big data to judge an individual's creditworthiness from odd signals: whether you type in all caps, or whether you anxiously keep your phone near 100% charge or let it run down to 3–4%.
stories.insight: Behavioural data lets firms make predictions about one person, which is Amit's case for 'a market of one'. Ajay's reply is that such models are still trained on a pooled group, so someone has to choose which group.
stories.quote: For example, your credit worthiness can actually be assessed by whether you type in all caps or not.

stories.topic: Nehru Writing History From a Prison Desk
stories.summary: Amit asks whether Nehru wrote The Discovery of India in prison. Ajay confirms he was in jail, though political prisoners were treated reasonably well. He had no library and no computer, only a couple of books on his desk that friends rotated in and out. Glimpses of World History, his letters to Indira Gandhi, was likewise written largely from memory.
stories.insight: These foundational books came out of what one mind could hold. Ajay adds that he only understood The Discovery of India when he reread it as an adult.
stories.quote: But it is true, he had no library, no computer. He just had a couple of books on his desk and his friends would be able to rotate books to him on that desk and he was writing.

recommendations.creator: Shrayana Bhattacharya
recommendations.context: Amit's recommendation at the end of the episode.
recommendations.reason: It uses Indian women's adoration of Shah Rukh Khan to show what Indian society is like and how lonely its women are. Amit says it 'contains multitudes': economics, sociology and beautiful writing, with Bollywood as the lens, much like this episode.

recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Shrayana Bhattacharya
recommendations.context: His conversation with Shrayana about her book.
recommendations.reason: It is his most popular episode ever. He chose the title on purpose because he thinks it is what the book is really about.

recommendations.creator: Vivian Gornick
recommendations.context: He discovered her through his conversation with Shrayana Bhattacharya.
recommendations.reason: He calls Gornick 'the great memoirist' and says all of her books are recommendations.

recommendations.item: The Loneliness of the Indian Man (Episode 303, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Nikhil Taneja
recommendations.context: His quiz to Ajay about his second most popular episode.
recommendations.reason: He calls this episode of more than seven hours 'a classic' and suggests listening to it alongside the episode on Indian women.

recommendations.item: The Loneliness of the Long-Distance Runner
recommendations.creator: Alan Sillitoe
recommendations.context: The title his 'Loneliness of…' episodes play on.
recommendations.reason: He calls it Sillitoe's 'great novel'. It is the inspiration behind his series of episode titles.

recommendations.item: The Loneliness of the Long-Distance Trucker (Episode 192, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Rajat Ubhaykar
recommendations.context: The first of his Sillitoe-inspired episode titles.
recommendations.reason: It is a conversation with Rajat Ubhaykar, who wrote a book about trucking across India.

recommendations.item: The Discovery of India
recommendations.creator: Jawaharlal Nehru
recommendations.context: Ajay's recommendation at the end of the episode, which he calls 'odd' because most Indians read it in childhood.
recommendations.reason: He read it at 12 and understood it only years later. Rereading it as an adult, he found it 'literally the book that invents the idea of India.' He urges adults who read it as children to go back to it. Amit adds that children should read it now and return to it later.

recommendations.item: Glimpses of World History
recommendations.creator: Jawaharlal Nehru
recommendations.context: Mentioned with The Discovery of India.
recommendations.reason: Nehru's letters to Indira Gandhi, a history of the world written from prison largely from memory.

recommendations.item: Is India a Flailing State?
recommendations.creator: Lant Pritchett
recommendations.context: The source of the metaphor Ajay applies to the old Indian firm.
recommendations.reason: Pritchett describes the Indian state as having a working brain whose nerves to the limbs are severed. Ajay uses this to explain why pre-1990s firms were coalitions of people doing their own thing.

recommendations.item: The Nature of the Firm
recommendations.creator: Ronald Coase
recommendations.context: Raised when Amit asks whether the design of firms needs rethinking.
recommendations.reason: Coase first asked why firms are centrally run inside while markets run on contracts and prices outside. That question is Ajay's starting point for asking whether today's firms need to be so centralised internally.

recommendations.item: Seeing Like a State
recommendations.creator: James C Scott
recommendations.context: Applied to national firms.
recommendations.reason: Scott's account of states that cannot see ground reality also fits big national firms, whose arrogance keeps them from seeing local needs.

recommendations.item: CMIE household data (Consumer Pyramids)
recommendations.creator: CMIE / Mahesh Vyas
recommendations.context: Ajay calls it 'one great learning experience' that opened his eyes to India's diversity.
recommendations.reason: It splits India into about 100 homogeneous regions and holds household survey data for each. Ajay is now 'a great enthusiast' of this way of seeing India instead of as one monolith or as states.

recommendations.item: In Service of the Republic
recommendations.creator: Vijay Kelkar and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: The comparisons of income and women's phone ownership across regions were homework for its decentralisation chapter.
recommendations.reason: It is where Ajay worked through the data on how diverse India is, which underpins his argument for decentralisation.

recommendations.item: Buying Maggi noodles and Kit Kats in every country you visit
recommendations.context: An aside while explaining that global brands localise their products.
recommendations.reason: 'It's great fun.' You taste first-hand how firms tailor one product to local preferences.

recommendations.creator: Gregory Lovvorn
recommendations.context: Show-notes link for Ajay's Kit Kat comparison.
recommendations.reason: Background on why the British Kit Kat that fans revere differs from the American one.

recommendations.reason: It shows how far one brand will go to localise for a single market.

recommendations.reason: It discusses lenders using individual behavioural data, such as typing in all caps or phone battery habits, to judge creditworthiness.

recommendations.creator: Sajith Pai
recommendations.context: Amit calls it 'much talked about' and promises to link it.
recommendations.reason: It divides Indians by income into a small affluent top, a middle class with middle-income-country lives, and a large base living like sub-Saharan Africa. Useful for anyone tempted to call India a market of 1.4 billion.

recommendations.context: Amit calls it 'a very popular one' on how firms evolve.

core_ideas.concept: Local → National → Adaptive: The Arc of the Indian Firm
core_ideas.explanation: Until the 1980s, Indian firms were national only in name. Branch managers ran their own operations because they couldn't be monitored. From the 1990s, IT and telecom produced the true national firm, with central processes and controls. Ajay argues the next stage must bring local responsiveness back, this time with central controls intact.
core_ideas.quote: Now Robert Clive was under the daily misery of surveillance from HQ.

core_ideas.explanation: Lant Pritchett describes the Indian state as a brain whose nerves to the fingers have been cut. Ajay applies this to the old Indian firm. HQ may have had a strategy, but each branch did its own thing, so the firm was really a coalition of individuals and couldn't carry out a strategy, manage risk or stop local corruption.
core_ideas.quote: it's a bit like the way Lant Pritchett describes the Indian state, that there is a brain, but the nerves have been severed and the fingers are doing their own thing.

core_ideas.concept: The Unnoticed Engine of India's Boom
core_ideas.explanation: The binding constraint on Indian business into the 1990s was telecom, which was either unavailable or absurdly expensive. Then trade barriers fell, computers got cheap and the Vajpayee-era reforms ended the Department of Telecom's stranglehold. A generation of managers used this to build national firms with central data, ERP systems, Andersen Consulting/Accenture-style process engineering and operational audits. Firms grew in scale and productivity without adding much labour. Ajay counts this as a core driver of GDP growth from 1991 to 2011 that hardly anyone talks about.
core_ideas.quote: all of us have lived it, we've just stopped noticing it, and I want to pull this out of our consciousness and say that this was big, this was huge.

core_ideas.explanation: Amit borrows the biologists' term for copying a practice simply because it worked elsewhere. Imported best practice made Indian firms more efficient but also more alike. Ajay agrees, but says the main channel was global firms' practices, not Indian business schools. In banking, for example, the template of a well-run foreign bank came in through foreign banks and people who had worked in them.
core_ideas.quote: And it's the same kind of ideas, the same kind of frameworks, and a lot of it is coming from the West with the danger of what biologists called isomorphic mimicry

core_ideas.explanation: CMIE groups India's roughly 700 districts into about 100 regions. Each is a contiguous cluster of about seven districts within one state, with similar women's literacy and agroclimatic zone, and holds about 14 million people. Ajay says state boundaries are 'kinda random', so this is the more useful unit. Measured this way, India is more diverse than Europe or Africa. Lant Pritchett once told Ajay that by some measures India's spread is wider than that of Latin America and Africa merged together.
core_ideas.quote: India is more diverse than Africa. India is more diverse than Europe.

core_ideas.concept: Localise Once the Market Can Pay for It
core_ideas.explanation: Global firms reformulate products country by country. As India grows towards the market size of an Indonesia or Thailand, it becomes worth customising within India too: first North versus South, then by state, then by homogeneous region. This applies to software, such as home-loan algorithms, as much as to food. How far to go is a strategy choice, but one design for the whole country is hard to justify.
core_ideas.quote: That really seems preposterous given the amount of diversity of India.

core_ideas.concept: No Customer of One Without a Pool
core_ideas.explanation: Amit argues Amazon and YouTube already personalise for each individual. Ajay replies that even a personal prediction comes from a model trained on many people's data. The real decision is which pool to train on: the world, India, South India, Tamil Nadu or one homogeneous region. Indian firms habitually choose all-India.
core_ideas.quote: But you can't make a prediction for a customer of one with a data set of one. So there will always be a certain amount of optimal pooling.

core_ideas.explanation: Like James C Scott's state, the big national firm can't perceive local reality. Despite trillion-rupee valuations, it serves only some income bands in each region and leaves much of the country unserved. That leaves room for well-adapted local firms, like a deeply optimised Rajasthan firm, even though the national firms have a cost of capital no one can match.
core_ideas.quote: It makes it difficult for the firm to see that reality.

core_ideas.concept: The Federated Firm: HQ as Treasury, Regions as Mini-CEOs
core_ideas.explanation: Multinationals already know Poland differs from France. Ajay proposes Indian firms borrow that approach. HQ keeps strategy, capital allocation, governance, the board and HR, plus non-negotiables like anti-money-laundering. Regional units own their P&L and adapt products, processes and models such as home-loan scoring. They compete for HQ capital on ROE. Firms range from Casio, which changes only local ads and distribution, to fully flexible designs. Whether to use 5, 20 or 100 regions depends on the firm's management capability relative to the diversity it faces.
core_ideas.quote: So the HQ will be the treasury, and the various sub firms all over India should be in an auction where they ask for capital and then they use it efficiently.

core_ideas.concept: Coase Reopened: Must the Inside of a Firm Be Stalinist?
core_ideas.explanation: Coase asked why firms are centrally run internally while the outside world runs on prices and contracts, which raises the question of where a firm's boundary should be. Ajay's modern question is whether the inside needs that much central control at all. Amit frames it as: if bottom-up order works for societies, how much of it can large firms copy?
core_ideas.quote: How come inside a firm we seem to run some Stalinist centralization, but outside the firm we live the world of contracts and flexibility of prices?

core_ideas.concept: India Is a Smaller Market Than 1.4 Billion
core_ideas.explanation: Amit summarises Sajith Pai's income tiers, giving rough figures. About 1–2 crore Indians are at the top, of whom 20–30 lakh are fully 'first world'. About 10 crore are middle class, living like people in middle-income countries; Amit says domestic workers and drivers belong here. The rest live like sub-Saharan Africa and often cannot even afford to migrate to a city for work. For some products, the real market is tiny.
core_ideas.quote: Depending on your product, it might only be a market of 20 lakhs.

core_ideas.concept: Profit Dispersion Reveals a Firm's Blind Spots
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's reply to the 'small market' view is to compute revenue or profit per capita, or ROE, for each homogeneous region. A wide interquartile range suggests a failure of the firm, not of the market. People in the weakest regions have some disposable income too, and serving them means dropping the one-product-for-all-India mindset.
core_ideas.quote: And if that's widely diverse, to some extent I'll turn around and blame the firm.

core_ideas.explanation: Amit points out that tastes are not tied to places: Tamils and Bengalis live all over India. He suggests firms could make many variants, ship all of them everywhere, and let local shopkeepers decide what to stock. Ajay agrees this is a real problem and compares it to travellers bringing back British or Japanese Kit Kats, or a Tamilian stocking up on podi in Chennai.
core_ideas.quote: So when you're thinking localization, you could be catering to a particular sliver of taste, which is, however, spread out geographically throughout.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: Amit's opening: Ajay will cover the Indian business landscape for the next 20 years ('Terribly exciting, isn't it?'), while Amit will 'talk about the boring subject of Bollywood.' He then asks viewers to picture Ajay, instead of Shah Rukh Khan, jumping around and singing in Baazigar, and suggests they use good AI to make that clip.

Amit calls Baazigar lyricist Zafar Gorakhpuri 'a great philosopher, and I'm saying this only on the basis of these words.' He presents 'Kitaben Bahut Si' as a magnificent dissertation couched in a song, proving that bookish knowledge is irrelevant and credentialism is nonsense.
Ajay protests, 'that is two videos already, and I ain't even got started.' Amit replies, 'Let me tell you something, Ajay Shah, I ain't even got started,' and cues a third.
Amit: 'I often say that India inhabits three centuries at the same time, 19th, 20th, 21st. But now I add a fourth to that list because your mind is in the 22nd century.'
Ajay on India's state boundaries: 'Like really should UP be one state? Okay, it makes no sense.'
When Ajay suggests hiring 'red-blooded North Indians', Amit objects: 'Everyone is red-blooded… I did not expect the sad stereotyping from you.'
After all the talk of variability and interquartile ranges, the Bollywood cue: 'Bollywood has done interquartile range. Watch.' A Ranbir Kapoor scene from Rocket Singh follows.
On Amit's run of 'Loneliness of…' episodes: 'It should have been Lonely Reader.' Amit concludes that he's done with the series because we're all lonely anyway.
On Nehru writing his histories from memory in prison with a few rotating books, Amit says: 'He would have been a podcaster today.'
Gangs of Wasseypur Part 2's 'Beta tumse na ho payega' scene, which Amit plays to depict HQ's disdain for the local manager who 'doesn't get it'.
Chak De India's 'Sirf ek naam sunayi deta hai' clash between a state-team captain and the coach of the Indian national women's team, used to set up the rise of the national firm.
'Main Aai Hoon U.P. Bihar Lootne' from Shool, which Amit plays as a nod to regional strategy: 'not quite' hyperlocal, but 'a step in the right direction.'
Sudheendra Kulkarni and N.K. Singh, whom Ajay credits with 'amazing things' in the Vajpayee years that 'blew up the death grip of the department of telecom on Indian Telecom.'
Andersen Consulting, now Accenture, whose time-and-motion and enterprise process engineering Ajay says spread across hundreds of Indian firms.
Mahesh Vyas and CMIE, behind the algorithm that divides India into about 100 homogeneous regions.
Alan Sillitoe's The Loneliness of the Long-Distance Runner, the template for Amit's Seen and the Unseen titles: the Long-Distance Trucker, the Indian Woman and the Indian Man.
